key_terms.meaning: A running program with its own memory, a PID, a parent and a state (running, sleeping, stopped, zombie).
Process ID: the unique positive integer the kernel assigns to each process; process 1 starts the rest.
A small numbered message sent to a process (SIGTERM = 15 asks it to end, SIGKILL = 9 forces it, SIGSTOP pauses it).
A finished child whose exit status the parent has not yet read, so its entry stays in the process table.
Scheduling priority hint from −20 (most CPU time) to 19 (least); set with nice or renice.
User ID: the number the kernel uses for a user's identity; UID 0 is root.
Root-only file holding password hashes and aging fields, readable by the kernel for login checks.
Runs one command as another user (default root) after checking /etc/sudoers, instead of logging in as root.
A signed, indexed server location holding packages and metadata that a package manager downloads from.
A package that another package needs to run, which the package manager installs automatically.
High-level package managers that resolve dependencies and call low-level tools (dpkg, rpm) to install .deb or .rpm files.
A .service/.socket/.target text file describing what to run, its dependencies and its restart rules.
Creates a symlink so the unit starts automatically at boot; it does not start the unit now.
Secure Shell: encrypted remote login and file copy on TCP port 22, with key-based authentication.
Network File System: exports a directory from a server so a client can mount it over the network.
Linux service that speaks SMB/CIFS so Windows clients can use Linux files and printers.
Software layer that runs guest operating systems; KVM is built into the Linux kernel, so it is a type-1 style hypervisor.
An isolated group of processes sharing the host kernel, with its own filesystem view and namespaces.
Mapping a host directory into a container's filesystem (for example -v /data:/data) so changes are visible on both sides.
Daemon that runs commands on a schedule read from crontab files, with fields minute, hour, day, month, weekday.

takeaways: Every running program is a process with a PID, a parent and a state, and you control it with signals rather than by hand.
SIGTERM is a polite request; SIGKILL cannot be caught and risks data loss, so it is the last step, not the first.
Users and groups give processes an identity and files an owner, so all access control starts with account management.
A package manager keeps software, dependencies and updates consistent by working from a signed repository instead of loose files.
systemd reads unit files; start and stop change the current state, while enable and disable change the state at the next boot.
Networking administration means knowing your address, mask, gateway and DNS, then testing reachability and remote access with ping and SSH.
NFS is the natural choice between Linux machines; Samba is needed when Windows clients must share files.
A container shares the host kernel and starts in seconds, while a KVM guest runs its own kernel and gives full isolation.
Automation scripts pay off only when they check exit status and log failures, because a silent cron job can stay broken for weeks.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask you to explain a mechanism and then show the exact commands, so pair each concept with the command, the file it changes and the output you would check.

bank.q: Define a process in Linux. Explain the states a process passes through and how ps and top display them.
outline: Process = running program plus its address space, PID, PPID, credentials and state
States: running (R), sleeping interruptible (S), uninterruptible (D), stopped (T), zombie (Z)
Every process except PID 1 has a parent; parent exit reparents children to PID 1
ps -ef lists PID, PPID, user, command; top adds CPU and memory use and refreshes
Zombie entries remain until the parent calls wait()

bank.q: Explain user and group management in Linux. Describe useradd, usermod and userdel and the files each one changes.
outline: Identity: UID for users, GID for groups, stored in /etc/passwd and /etc/group
useradd writes passwd, group, shadow and creates or skips home directory (-m, -s, -G)
passwd sets or locks the password hash in /etc/shadow
usermod changes shell, home, groups or comment; userdel -r removes home directory
Primary group versus supplementary groups; file ownership uses one user and one group

bank.q: Explain how a package manager installs a package from a repository, including dependency resolution and removal.
outline: Repository index lists package name, version, dependencies and checksums
apt update refreshes index; apt install name downloads package plus unmet dependencies
dpkg or rpm does the actual unpacking and script running
Database of installed files allows clean removal and upgrades
apt remove keeps configuration; purge deletes it; autoremove clears unused dependencies

bank.q: What is a systemd unit file? Explain the sections [Unit], [Service] and [Install] and the meaning of start, stop, enable and disable.
outline: Unit file is a plain text description of a service, socket or target
[Unit] holds Description and ordering/requirement settings such as After=
[Service] holds ExecStart, ExecStop, Restart and User
[Install] holds WantedBy=multi-user.target used when enabling
start and stop change the current state; enable and disable change the boot-time symlinks

bank.q: Explain IP address, subnet mask, default gateway and DNS in Linux, and describe how ping tests reachability.
outline: IPv4 address identifies an interface; the mask separates network and host bits
Default gateway is the router used for addresses outside the local subnet
ip addr shows addresses, ip route shows the routing table
DNS server maps names to addresses; /etc/resolv.conf or systemd-resolved holds it
ping sends ICMP echo requests and reports round-trip time and loss; ICMP may be blocked by firewalls

bank.q: A process has stopped responding on a server. Show the commands you would use to identify it, terminate it in stages, and explain why kill -9 should be the last option.
outline: ps -ef or top or pgrep to find the PID and confirm it is the right process
kill -15 PID sends SIGTERM so the program can save data and clean up
Check again with ps; if still present, send kill -9 PID (SIGKILL, cannot be caught)
If it will not die in uninterruptible sleep (D), the cause is usually I/O or a stuck mount
SIGKILL skips cleanup: open files, temp files and database writes may be left inconsistent

bank.q: Write the commands to create a group accounts, add users ravi and meena to it, lock meena's account, and give a shared directory group ownership and the right permissions.
outline: groupadd accounts
useradd -m -G accounts ravi and the same for meena
passwd -l meena locks the hash; passwd -u unlocks
chgrp accounts /srv/shared and chmod 2770 /srv/shared
Setgid bit keeps new files in the same group; umask affects default permissions

bank.q: Describe step by step how you would set up passwordless SSH from a laptop to a server, and then mount an NFS export from that server.
outline: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 on the client creates a key pair
ssh-copy-id user@server appends the public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
Check permissions: ~/.ssh 700 and authorized_keys 600
On the server add the export to /etc/exports and run exportfs -ra
On the client apt install nfs-common, then mount -t nfs server:/export /mnt; mount -a for fstab entries

bank.q: Write a Python script that runs a shell command, checks its exit status, writes a timestamped log line, and run it every day at 2:30 a.m. using cron.
outline: subprocess.run([...], capture_output=True, text=True) returns a CompletedProcess
returncode 0 means success; non-zero means failure, and stderr holds the message
Write the log with open('log.txt','a') and a datetime.now() timestamp
Make it executable with a shebang line #!/usr/bin/env python3
crontab -e entry: 30 2 * * * /usr/bin/python3 /home/user/job.py

bank.q: Compare a Docker container with a KVM guest under the headings kernel, isolation, startup time, storage and typical use, and say when you would choose each.
outline: Container shares the host kernel; KVM guest boots its own kernel
Isolation: namespaces and cgroups versus hardware-assisted full virtual machine
Startup: seconds for a container, tens of seconds for a guest
Storage: image layers and volumes versus a disk image file or block device
Containers suit packaging one service; KVM suits different kernels, full OS testing and stronger separation

bank.q: A service responds to systemctl start but does not come back after a reboot. Analyse the possible states of the unit and the commands you would use to find and fix the cause.
outline: systemctl status shows active/inactive and enabled/disabled separately
A unit can be running but not enabled, or enabled but failed at boot
systemctl is-enabled and systemctl is-active answer each question
journalctl -u name and -b show the boot-time error
Fix by systemctl enable name, correcting the unit file, or resolving a failed dependency with After=/Requires=

bank.q: A web service on a Linux server is down after a package upgrade and a new firewall rule. Using tools from process, package, service and network administration, lay out a diagnostic order and justify it.
outline: Check the service first: systemctl status and journalctl -u for the error message
Check the process layer: is the process running, what PID, what user, any zombie or crash loop
Check the package layer: recent upgrades, config file changes, held-back dependencies
Check the network layer: listening ports with ss -lntp, firewall rules, ping and remote reachability
Justify bottom-up or top-down order, restore service, then make the fix permanent

bank.q: Compare NFS and Samba for sharing files across a mixed Linux and Windows network. Discuss configuration files, authentication and security concerns for each.
outline: NFS: /etc/exports on the server, mount on the client, suits Linux to Linux
Samba: /etc/samba/smb.conf, SMB/CIFS protocol, suits Windows clients
Authentication: NFS commonly trusts host or Kerberos; Samba uses its own user database or AD
Security: restrict exports by subnet, avoid no_root_squash, control SMB signing and guest access
Firewall ports: 2049 for NFS, 445 and 139 for SMB

bank.q: A nightly backup must run unattended. Evaluate running it as a Python script from cron, as a systemd timer, or inside a container, and state which you would choose with reasons.
outline: cron: simple crontab line, no dependency handling, thin logging, poor handling of missed runs
systemd timer: logs in journal, can run after boot or after another unit, catches up with Persistent=true
Container: reproducible environment and dependencies, but needs volume or bind mount for the backup target
All three need exit status checks and alerting; silent failure is the main risk
Choice depends on environment: existing systemd hosts favour timers, portable jobs favour containers

glossary.def: A background process with no controlling terminal that provides a service, usually named with a trailing d such as sshd.
A command that holds the terminal until it finishes; suspend it with Ctrl+Z and resume with fg or bg.
A shell command that sends a signal by number or name to a PID; it is not limited to killing.
The kernel's list of all current processes, visible through /proc and ps.
An interactive viewer of processes sorted by CPU use, refreshed every few seconds.
World-readable file with one line per user: name, UID, GID, home directory and login shell.
A named set of users with one GID, used to grant the same file permissions to many people.
The group recorded against a user in /etc/passwd; new files take this group by default.
The superuser with UID 0, who bypasses ordinary permission checks.
A single installable archive of files plus metadata such as name, version and dependencies.
Low-level tools that unpack and register one package file without fetching dependencies.
Downloads fresh repository index files so the package manager knows current versions.
The command used to start, stop, enable, disable and inspect systemd units.
A systemd unit that groups other units, roughly replacing the older runlevel idea.
Reads the systemd journal, the main place to look for why a service failed.
A 32-bit pattern that marks which bits of an IPv4 address are network bits and which are host bits.
The router address used to reach destinations that are not on the local subnet.
A 16-bit number that selects the service on a host, for example 22 for SSH and 80 for HTTP.
A directory that an NFS server makes available to named client hosts, listed in /etc/exports.
A read-only template of a container filesystem, built in layers and started as one or more containers.
Docker-managed storage that survives the removal of a container, kept outside the image.
Kernel-based Virtual Machine: Linux's built-in hypervisor using CPU virtualization extensions.
The number a process returns on exit; 0 means success and non-zero means some kind of failure.
A per-user file of schedule lines that the cron daemon reads to run commands automatically.
